title: Four homes per lot and housing affordability strategy
subtitle: Also: downtown building heights study, 8 Mitchell Street rezoning, Rutherford Conservatory deconstruction and the Carden Street heritage designation.
overview: Council approved zoning and Official Plan changes that allow up to four dwelling units on low density residential lots across Guelph {{vote:m6}}. A requirement that extra units on corner lots be set back as far as the main house passed {{vote:m4}}. A proposal to require one parking space per unit was defeated {{vote:m5}}. Staff said the reduced parking rules support the city's federal housing funding commitments.

Council also approved the 2024 Housing Affordability Strategy and a related Official Plan amendment setting new affordable housing targets {{vote:m9}}. An amendment moved action 2.1.1, on protecting existing affordable housing, into the high priority actions, with staff to report back in March 2025 {{vote:m8}}. Many delegates spoke about deeply affordable housing, vacant homes, renovictions and housing for people with disabilities.

Council directed staff to begin the downtown building heights study {{vote:m12}} and approved the 8 Mitchell Street rezoning for semi-detached homes {{vote:m16}}. It approved deconstruction of the Rutherford Conservatory on condition that salvageable steel be kept for a commemorative structure {{vote:m19}}. A heritage designation by-law for 106 Carden Street was also approved {{vote:m2}}. After the closed session, the Mayor reported that council received information and gave direction to staff on the 201 Elmira Road S. Ontario Land Tribunal matter.

decisions.detail: Council approved an Official Plan amendment and a zoning by-law amendment, as amended, permitting up to four units on low density residential lots {{vote:m6}}.

decisions.item: Corner lot setback for additional units
decisions.detail: Council required additional dwelling units to be set back from the exterior side lot line at least as far as the main dwelling {{vote:m4}}.
Council approved the final 2024 Housing Affordability Strategy, as amended, and Official Plan Amendment No. 101 setting new affordable housing targets {{vote:m9}}.
Action 2.1.1 moves into the high priority actions, with staff to report back with an approach and schedule in March 2025 {{vote:m8}}.
Staff were directed to proceed with the Section 26 Official Plan update to start the downtown building heights study {{vote:m12}}.
Council approved rezoning from Neighbourhood Institutional to a specialized low density residential zone to permit semi-detached dwellings {{vote:m16}}.

Council approved deconstruction on condition that salvageable steel be kept for a commemorative structure, and encouraged the University of Guelph to reuse limestone and glass in the garden {{vote:m19}}.
Council received the owner's objection and approved the designation by-law {{vote:m2}}.

debate: On four units per lot, staff said reduced parking was the main way to enable about 3,000 more eligible lots and was tied to the city's housing funding agreement. One councillor raised concerns about street parking in tight neighbourhoods, while others said reduced parking was needed to unlock housing.

On the parking amendment, its mover argued parking could not be added back later and that rules could be revisited. Opponents said it could put federal funding or a future funding opportunity at risk through appeals. Staff said they would need to confirm with the federal housing agency, and that the risk was mainly of an appeal delaying the by-law.

On the Housing Affordability Strategy, delegates asked for a vacant home tax and a renovation by-law to be made higher priority. Others asked for acquisition funds for community land trusts and for explicit measures for people with disabilities and low incomes. Staff said the priority order reflected how quickly actions could add units and that all actions remain important. Several delegates were told to keep remarks to the report.

On 8 Mitchell Street, nearby residents raised parking, tree loss, building design and heritage character, and asked for the word "may" to become "shall" for four extra parking spaces. Staff said the planning legislation limits what the city can require and that the change could invite an appeal. The amendment was defeated {{vote:m14}}.

On the Rutherford Conservatory, Heritage Guelph and several delegates opposed demolition and cited its heritage value. The university said repair would cost more than $5 million and that snow loads made the structure a safety risk. Councillors weighed the risk of an appeal against the heritage value.
